reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A fibromuscular membrane divides the left atrium into a proximal chamber receiving the pulmonary veins and a distal chamber containing the appendage and mitral valve
Haemodynamics mimic mitral stenosis, with pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary hypertension and, in severe cases, low cardiac output
Severity depends on the size of the communicating orifice in the membrane; a small orifice presents in infancy while a large one may be silent until adulthood
Presentation ranges from breathlessness, recurrent chest infections and failure to thrive in infants to exertional dyspnoea or atrial arrhythmia in older patients
The dividing membrane sits above the level of the atrial appendage and fossa ovalis, distinguishing it from a supravalvar mitral ring
Associated lesions include atrial septal defect and anomalous pulmonary venous connection, which may modify the clinical picture
Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the obstructing membrane, which usually gives excellent relief when performed before fixed pulmonary vascular changes develop
reference.pathophysiology: Cor triatriatum sinister arises when a fibromuscular membrane partitions the left atrium into a posterosuperior chamber that receives the pulmonary veins and an anteroinferior chamber bearing the left atrial appendage and mitral valve. The embryological basis is incomplete incorporation of the common pulmonary vein into the left atrium. Blood must cross a restrictive orifice within the membrane, producing an obstruction functionally equivalent to mitral stenosis. The upstream chamber and pulmonary veins become congested, pulmonary venous and then pulmonary arterial pressures rise, and right heart pressure loading follows. The degree of obstruction, and hence age at presentation, is governed by the diameter of the communicating orifice and any associated atrial septal communication that may decompress the proximal chamber.
additionalDifferentials: Total or partial anomalous pulmonary venous return
Left atrial myxoma or other mass
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography to visualise the dividing membrane and measure the orifice gradient
Doppler assessment of flow across the membrane and estimation of pulmonary artery pressure
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define pulmonary venous connections and chamber anatomy
Chest radiograph to assess pulmonary venous congestion and cardiac silhouette
Cardiac catheterisation when pulmonary vascular resistance or coexisting lesions need clarification
Electrocardiogram to detect right ventricular hypertrophy or atrial arrhythmia
redFlags: Severe pulmonary venous congestion or pulmonary oedema in a distressed infant
Signs of low cardiac output or shock from critical membrane obstruction
New atrial arrhythmia with haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: Surgical resection of the membrane is generally curative with low operative mortality and an excellent long-term outlook when performed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Untreated severe obstruction in infancy carries high mortality.
pitfalls: Mistaking the obstructing membrane for congenital mitral stenosis or a supravalvar ring, which changes surgical planning
Overlooking a small membrane orifice because a coexisting atrial septal defect masks the pressure gradient
Attributing an infant's respiratory distress to recurrent infection rather than pulmonary venous obstruction
Failing to search for associated anomalous pulmonary venous connections
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Surgical resection of the obstructing intra-atrial membrane is the definitive and generally curative treatment when obstruction is significant
Stabilise symptomatic pulmonary venous congestion pre-operatively with diuretics and, in critically obstructed infants, urgent surgical referral
Repair associated lesions such as atrial septal defect or anomalous pulmonary venous connection at the time of surgery
Manage atrial arrhythmia with rate or rhythm control and anticoagulation as indicated
Undertake postoperative echocardiographic surveillance for residual or recurrent obstruction and pulmonary pressure recovery
Coordinate care through a congenital cardiology and cardiac surgery multidisciplinary team
Escalate promptly for severe infantile obstruction, which carries high mortality if untreated
